title: Investigate and harden against GPU capacity surge from KV-cache fragmentation and tenant hotspotting
creator: Liam Chen
description: Summary: Last week's hosted API incident revealed recurring GPU pool exhaustion driven by two compounding signals: (1) KV-cache fragmentation across long-running sessions causing increased memory footprint and reduced packing efficiency, and (2) a small set of tenants generating hotspot traffic with large prefix mismatch leading to queue amplification. These factors led autoscaler hysteresis to under-react and our admission controls to amplify queue growth instead of trimming demand. Goal: drive a set of low-risk mitigations for the next 2 sprints to reduce outage probability and improve detection/response; plus a medium-term plan for runtime changes to KV cache compaction and tenant-aware admission scoring.
reproduction_steps: Simulate 20% of requests with long-lived chat sessions that warm KV for 1,500-token prefixes, interleave short requests from other tenants to cause KV fragmentation.
Replay load from post-incident capture (s3://redwood-incident-captures/2026-03-02/gpu-spike) against a 12-GPU pool with current runtime settings.
Introduce an artificial tenant that emits bursty 80% of tokens with unique prefixes to stress packing and queueing.
Measure queue_length, token_throughput, kv_cache_hit_rate, autoscaler_decision_latency, and admission_drop_rate.
Observe that average GPU memory utilization approaches 98% while CPU-side request queue grows and autoscaler waits full cooldown period before scaling.
observations: KV cache fragmentation increases per-request memory by ~14% for long-lived sessions vs baseline.
Top 5 tenants accounted for 62% of the queue during the event; multi-tenant mixing reduced batching efficiency.
Autoscaler cooldown/hysteresis prevented rapid scale-up; prewarm bias assumes steady-state not bursty hotspots.
Admission control currently uses token-rate only; lacks tenant-aware fairness and cache-affinity signals.
Telemetry lag: metrics aggregation window (30s) delayed detection of rapid queue growth.

decisions: Short-term (1 sprint): implement tenant-aware soft admission that reduces new-slot admission for tenants with high kv_cache_fragmentation_score.
Short-term: lower autoscaler scale-up cooldown and add rapid-probe scaler mode for hotspot detection.
Short-term: add a queue-length-derived emergency throttle that caps low-priority traffic when pool memory > 92%.
Medium-term (2-3 sprints): implement KV cache compaction/background-eviction for long-lived sessions and expose cache-affinity hints to admission.
Medium-term: add tenant-scorer to the admission pipeline that combines recent queue contribution, cache-locality, and success-rate regression.
Telemetry: emit 5s sliding-window metrics for queue growth and autoscaler response time.

risks: Tenant-aware admission could unfairly penalize high-value customers if scoring is inaccurate — need canary and opt-out path for enterprise customers.
Reducing autoscaler cooldown increases chance of oscillation; mitigate by capping scale-down aggressiveness and adding smoothing for scale-down.
Emergency throttle risks degraded latency for low-priority workloads; require clear SLO docs and customer communication plan.
rollout_plan: Feature-flag all admission and autoscaler changes in runtime behind 'tenant_admission_v2' and 'autoscaler_probe_mode'.
Canary rollout: enable for 5% of traffic (non-enterprise) in us-west-2 for 24 hours, observe queue metrics and error budgets.
If canary stable, increase to 25% for 6 hours and validate telemetry and billing metrics.
Enterprise opt-out: provide ability to pin customers to legacy admission for first month after rollout.
test_plan: Unit tests for tenant scoring math and eviction thresholds.
Integration tests: run incident capture replay and assert queue length reduction and memory utilization drop.
Load tests: staging chaos job 'tenant-hotspot-sim' to verify autoscaler rapid-probe response and emergency throttle behavior.
Post-deploy regression suite to ensure no perf regressions for small-request cold-start patterns.
